units.title: Hello, Scala
units.summary: Write your first Scala program, print text with println and print, and join strings.

lesson.md: Every Scala program needs a starting point. The line `@main def run(): Unit =` creates it. `def` defines a function, `run` is its name, the empty parentheses `()` mean it takes no input, `: Unit` means it gives back no useful value, and `=` says that the body follows. `@main` marks this function as the place where the program starts.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  println("Hello, Scala!")

lesson.md: The body is the indented code below the first line. `println` prints the text in the parentheses and then starts a new line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, Scala!"`, is called a **string**. Each `println` prints its own line, from top to bottom.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  println("Good morning")
  println("Scala is fun")
  println("Bye")
lesson.output:
Good morning
Scala is fun
Bye

lesson.md: `print` works like `println`, but it does not start a new line. The next output continues on the same line. `println()` with nothing in the parentheses only starts a new line.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  print("Hello, ")
  print("Scala")
  println("!")
  println("Done")

lesson.md: Numbers are written without quotes, and Scala can calculate with them: `2 + 3` gives `5`. Inside quotes, `"2 + 3"` is only text and is printed as it is. With strings, `+` joins them into one string.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  println(2 + 3)
  println("2 + 3")
  println(10 * 4)
  println("Hello, " + "world")

lesson.md: Scala 3 uses indentation to group code. All lines of the body must start with the same number of spaces. Two spaces is the usual style. Older Scala code puts the body in curly braces `{` and `}` instead.
Scala is case-sensitive: `println` works, but `Println` or `PrintLn` is an error. A string also needs a double quote at the start and at the end.

card: `@main def run(): Unit =` starts the program
Indent the body, usually by 2 spaces

exercises.prompt: Which line prints Hello on its own line?
exercises.explain: `println` prints the string in the parentheses and then starts a new line. The other commands do not exist in Scala.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print?
exercises.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  print("Sca")
  print("la")
  println("!")
exercises.explain: `print` does not start a new line, so all three parts end up on one line: `Scala!`.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print?
exercises.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  println(6 * 7)
exercises.explain: Without quotes, `6 * 7` is a calculation. `*` multiplies, so Scala prints `42`.

exercises.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  println("3 + 4")
exercises.explain: The calculation is inside double quotes, so it is only text. The program prints `3 + 4`.

exercises.explain: `println` starts a new line after `Hi`. With `print`, the output would be `HiBye`.

exercises.explain: In Scala, functions are defined with `def`. `fun` and `func` are keywords of other languages.

exercises.explain: `println( 2 + 3 )` calculates `2 + 3` and prints `5`. Spaces next to the parentheses do not matter.

exercises.explain: The program starts with `@main def run(): Unit =`. The `println` lines run from top to bottom.

prints Hi without a new line

exercises.explain: The string `"Middle` has no closing double quote. Correct: `println("Middle")`.

exercises.prompt: Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: Scala is case-sensitive. `Println` does not exist; write `println("Bye")`.

exercises.prompt: In `@main def run(): Unit =`, what does `Unit` mean?
options: The function gives back no useful value
The function gives back a number
exercises.explain: The type after the colon is the type of the result. `Unit` means that there is no useful result: `run` only does something, like printing.

units.title: Values and types
units.summary: Store data with val and var, and get to know Int, Double, Boolean, String and type inference.

lesson.md: A **value** gives a name to a piece of data. You write `val`, the name, `=` and the data. After that, you can use the name instead of the data. A `val` can never change.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val name = "Mia"
  val age = 25
  println(name)
  println(age)

lesson.md: When something needs to change, use `var` for a **variable**. You give it a new value with `=`. `score += 5` is short for `score = score + 5`; `-=` and `*=` work the same way.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  var score = 10
  println(score)
  score = 15
  println(score)
  score += 5
  println(score)

lesson.md: Giving a `val` a new value is an error: the program does not compile and Scala reports `Reassignment to val`. Use `val` by default and `var` only when the value really has to change.

Every value has a **type**. `Int` is a whole number, `Double` is a number with decimals, `Boolean` is `true` or `false`, and `String` is text. Usually Scala works out the type by itself; this is called **type inference**. You can also write the type after a colon: `val age: Int = 25`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val count: Int = 3
  val price: Double = 2.5
  val open: Boolean = true
  val city: String = "Oslo"
  println(count)
  println(price)
  println(open)
  println(city)

lesson.md: Scala calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` (multiply) and `/` (divide). `%` gives the remainder of a division. Be careful: when you divide two `Int` values, the result is an `Int` too, and the decimals are cut off. If one of the numbers is a `Double`, the result has decimals.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  println(7 + 2)
  println(7 - 2)
  println(7 * 2)
  println(7 / 2)
  println(7 % 2)
  println(7.0 / 2)

lesson.md: To change the type of a value, use a conversion: `toDouble` turns a number into a `Double`, `toInt` turns a `Double` into an `Int` and cuts off the decimals, and `toInt` on a string like `"42"` reads the number in it.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val n = 7
  println(n.toDouble)
  val x = 9.8
  println(x.toInt)
  val text = "42"
  println(text.toInt + 1)

lesson.md: A type mismatch is an error. `val age: Int = "25"` does not compile, because `"25"` is a `String`, not an `Int`. Scala finds such mistakes before the program runs.

exercises.prompt: Which keyword creates a variable that you can change later?
exercises.explain: A `var` can get a new value with `=`. A `val` can never change.

  println(17 / 5)
exercises.explain: Both numbers are `Int` values, so the result is an `Int`. `17 / 5` is `3.4`, and the decimals are cut off: `3`.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print?
exercises.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  println(17 % 5)
exercises.explain: `%` gives the remainder. `5` fits into `17` three times (`15`), and `2` is left over.

exercises.code:

  val a = 10
  var b = a
  b += 5
  println(a + b)
exercises.explain: `b` starts as `10` and becomes `15`. `a` stays `10`. `10 + 15` is `25`.

exercises.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val n = 5
  n = 6
  println(n)
exercises.explain: `n` is a `val`, so it cannot get a new value. The program does not compile. With `var n = 5` it would print `6`.

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap with the right type.
exercises.explain: `4.5` has decimals, so its type is `Double`. An `Int` can only hold whole numbers.

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 3.

  count ___ 2
  println(count)
exercises.explain: `count += 2` adds `2` to `count`, so it becomes `3`. `count = 2` would set it to `2`, and `==` only compares.

exercises.prompt: Create a value named age of type Int with the value 30 that can never change.
exercises.explain: `val age: Int = 30` creates a value that cannot change. The type comes after the colon and starts with a capital letter.

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 12.
exercises.explain: `total` starts at `2`, `2 * 3` is `6`, and `6 + 6` is `12`. In the other order, `(2 + 6) * 3` would be `24`.

exercises.explain: `"25"` is a `String`, but `age` must be an `Int`. Write the number without quotes: `val age: Int = 25`.

exercises.prompt: Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: `price` is a `Double`, and Scala does not turn it into an `Int` by itself. Convert it: `val whole: Int = price.toInt`.

units.title: Strings
units.summary: Build text with s-interpolation and use length, toUpperCase, contains and substring.

lesson.md: A `String` is text in double quotes. You already know that `+` joins strings. When you join a string and a number, Scala turns the number into text: `"Age: " + 36` gives `"Age: 36"`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val first = "Ada"
  val last = "Lovelace"
  println(first + " " + last)
  println("Age: " + 36)

lesson.md: An easier way to build text is **string interpolation**. Write the letter `s` right before the opening quote. Inside the string, `$name` puts in the value of `name`. For a calculation or a longer expression, use curly braces: `${age + 1}`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val name = "Leo"
  val age = 20
  println(s"Hello, $name!")
  println(s"Next year you are ${age + 1}.")
lesson.output:
Hello, Leo!
Next year you are 21.

lesson.md: Do not forget the `s` before the quote. Without it, Scala prints `$name` as plain text and does not put in the value.

Strings have many **methods**: functions that belong to a value. You call them with a dot after the value. `length` counts the characters, `toUpperCase` and `toLowerCase` change capital letters, and `contains` checks if a text is inside the string. `contains` gives a `Boolean`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val word = "Scala"
  println(word.length)
  println(word.toUpperCase)
  println(word.toLowerCase)
  println(word.contains("ca"))
  println(word.contains("x"))

lesson.md: Every character in a string has a position, called its **index**. The first character has index `0`. `substring(start, end)` gives the characters from index `start` up to, but not including, index `end`. `substring(start)` goes to the end of the string. `replace` swaps one text for another.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val text = "Hello, Scala"
  println(text.substring(0, 5))
  println(text.substring(7))
  println(text.replace("Hello", "Hi"))

lesson.md: A string never changes. Methods like `toUpperCase` give back a **new** string, and the original string stays the same. To keep the result, store it in a new `val`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val city = "rome"
  val big = city.toUpperCase
  println(city)
  println(big)

The string has no `s` before the quote, so `$name` stays plain text. The program prints `Hello, $name`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Make decisions with if, then and else, compare and combine conditions, and choose with match.

lesson.md: A comparison gives a `Boolean`: `true` or `false`. Scala has `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `<=` (less than or equal) and `>=` (greater than or equal). You can compare strings with `==` too.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val age = 17
  println(age >= 18)
  println(age == 17)
  println(age != 17)
  println("cat" == "cat")

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. Write `if`, the condition, `then`, and the code below it, indented. The `else` part is optional: it runs when the condition is `false`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val temperature = 25
  if temperature > 20 then
    println("It is warm.")
  else
    println("It is cold.")

lesson.md: With `else if` you can check more conditions, one after the other. Scala runs the code of the first condition that is `true` and skips the rest.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val score = 72
  if score >= 90 then
    println("Grade A")
  else if score >= 70 then
    println("Grade B")
  else
    println("Grade C")

lesson.md: In Scala, `if` is an **expression**: it gives back a value. You can store this value in a `val`. Short ones fit on one line: `if a > b then a else b` gives `a` when `a` is bigger, otherwise `b`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val a = 8
  val b = 5
  val max = if a > b then a else b
  println(max)
  val label = if max % 2 == 0 then "even" else "odd"
  println(label)

lesson.md: **Logical operators** combine conditions. `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are true. `||` (or) is `true` when at least one side is true. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val age = 25
  val hasTicket = true
  println(age >= 18 && hasTicket)
  println(age < 12 || age > 65)
  println(!hasTicket)

lesson.md: `match` compares one value with several patterns. Each `case` has a pattern, an arrow `=>` and a result. Scala checks the cases from top to bottom and takes the first one that fits. `|` puts several values into one case, and `_` fits every value, so it goes last. Like `if`, `match` gives back a value.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val day = 6
  val name = day match
    case 1 => "Monday"
    case 6 | 7 => "Weekend"
    case _ => "Workday"
  println(name)
  val n = -4
  val sign = n match
    case 0 => "zero"
    case x if x > 0 => "positive"
    case _ => "negative"
  println(sign)

lesson.md: In the second `match`, `case x if x > 0` gives the value the name `x` and adds a condition, called a **guard**. The case fits only when the guard is `true`.

card: `val max = if a > b then a else b`

units.title: Loops and ranges
units.summary: Repeat code with for and while, count with ranges like 1 to 5, and build new collections with yield.

lesson.md: A `for` loop repeats code. `1 to 3` is a **range**: the numbers `1`, `2` and `3`, including the last one. In `for i <- 1 to 3 do`, the arrow `<-` takes each number from the range, one after the other, and gives it the name `i`. The code after `do` runs once for each number.

`until` makes a range **without** the last number: `0 until 3` is `0`, `1` and `2`. With `by` you choose the step: `1 to 10 by 3` counts `1`, `4`, `7`, `10`. A short loop body can stay on the same line as `do`.
To collect a result, create a `var` before the loop and change it inside the loop. Here `total` adds up the numbers from `1` to `4`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  var total = 0
  for n <- 1 to 4 do
    total += n
  println(total)

lesson.md: A `while` loop repeats its code as long as a condition is `true`. Scala checks the condition before every round. Inside the loop, you must change something so that the condition becomes `false` one day. `count -= 1` makes `count` one smaller.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  var count = 3
  while count > 0 do
    println(count)
    count -= 1
  println("Go!")

lesson.md: If the condition of a `while` loop never becomes `false`, the loop never ends. Check that the loop changes the variable in the condition.

With `yield` instead of `do`, a `for` loop does not run code but builds a **new collection**: one result for each value. For a range, the result is a `Vector`, a collection that holds values in order. `println` shows it as `Vector(…)`.
To count down, use a negative step: `for i <- 3 to 1 by -1 do` counts `3`, `2`, `1`. A range like `3 to 1` without a step is empty, so the loop does not run at all.

card: `1 to 10 by 2` counts in steps of 2

exercises.explain: `1 to 4` includes `4`. `print` does not start a new line, so the numbers end up next to each other.

exercises.explain: `n` goes from `10` to `5`, then `2`, then `1`. Now `n > 1` is `false`. That makes `3` rounds.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with def, parameters and return types, use default arguments and lambdas.

lesson.md: A **function** is a piece of code with a name that you can use again and again. You define it with `def`, the name, the **parameters** in parentheses and the return type after a colon. Every parameter needs a type. The value of the code after `=` is the result; you do not need a `return` keyword.

lesson.code:
def square(n: Int): Int = n * n

@main def run(): Unit =
  println(square(4))
  println(square(9))

lesson.md: Parameters are separated by commas. When you call the function, the **arguments** go into the parameters in the same order. A body with several lines is indented, and the last line gives the result.
A function that only does something, like printing, has the return type `Unit`. You call it on its own line.

A parameter can have a **default value**, written with `=` in the parameter list. When you leave out that argument, Scala uses the default. With **named arguments** like `greeting = "Hey"`, you say which parameter gets which value, in any order.

lesson.output:
Hello, Ana!
Hi, Ben!
Hey, Cy!

lesson.md: A **lambda** is a function without a name. `(x: Int) => x * 2` takes `x` and gives back `x * 2`. The arrow `=>` separates the parameters from the result. You can store a lambda in a `val` and call it like any function. Its type is written `Int => Int`: it takes an `Int` and gives back an `Int`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val double = (x: Int) => x * 2
  val add = (a: Int, b: Int) => a + b
  println(double(5))
  println(add(2, 3))

lesson.md: A function can take another function as a parameter. `applyTwice` below calls `f` two times. You can pass a stored lambda or write a new one directly in the call. In the call, `x => x + 10` needs no type, because Scala knows that `f` takes an `Int`.
Scala can often work out the return type by itself, so `def square(n: Int) = n * n` also works. Writing the return type makes your code easier to read and helps the compiler find mistakes.

card: The last expression is the result
`def f(x: Int = 1)` has a default value
`Unit`: the function gives back nothing useful

units.title: Lists and maps
units.summary: Keep many values in a List or a Map, and work with them using map, filter, sum and foreach.

lesson.md: A `List` holds several values in a fixed order. You create it with `List(…)` and the values separated by commas. `fruits(0)` gives the element at index `0`, the first one. `length` counts the elements, and `contains` checks if a value is in the list.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val fruits = List("apple", "banana", "cherry")
  println(fruits)
  println(fruits(0))
  println(fruits.length)
  println(fruits.contains("kiwi"))

lesson.md: A list never changes. `:+` gives back a **new** list with one more element at the end; the old list stays the same. With a `for` loop, you can go through all elements of a list.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val nums = List(3, 5)
  val more = nums :+ 8
  println(more)
  println(nums)
  for n <- more do
    println(n * 10)

lesson.md: `map` uses a function on every element and gives back a new list with the results. `filter` keeps only the elements for which the function gives `true`. `sum` adds all numbers. Instead of `x => x + 1`, you can write `_ + 1`: the `_` stands for the element.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val nums = List(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
  println(nums.map(x => x * 2))
  println(nums.filter(x => x % 2 == 0))
  println(nums.sum)
  println(nums.map(_ + 1))

lesson.md: You can call several methods one after the other. `foreach` runs a function for every element, for example `println`. `mkString` joins all elements into one string, with the text you give between them.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val prices = List(4, 12, 7, 20)
  val big = prices.filter(_ > 5).map(_ * 2)
  println(big)
  big.foreach(println)
  println(prices.mkString(" | "))

lesson.md: A `Map` stores pairs of a **key** and a **value**. `"Ana" -> 31` makes a pair with the key `"Ana"` and the value `31`. `ages("Ana")` gives the value for a key. `getOrElse` gives a default value when the key is missing. `+` gives back a new map with one more pair, and `size` counts the pairs.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val ages = Map("Ana" -> 31, "Ben" -> 25)
  println(ages("Ana"))
  println(ages.getOrElse("Cy", 0))
  val more = ages + ("Cy" -> 40)
  println(more.size)
  println(more)

lesson.md: A `for` loop can go through a map, too. In `for (fruit, count) <- stock do`, each pair is split into two names: `fruit` for the key and `count` for the value.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val stock = Map("apple" -> 3, "pear" -> 0)
  for (fruit, count) <- stock do
    println(s"$fruit: $count")

lesson.md: `ages("Zoe")` stops the program with an error when the key `"Zoe"` is missing. Use `getOrElse` when you are not sure that a key exists.

units.title: Case classes and Option
units.summary: Group data in case classes, add methods, take values apart with match, and handle missing values with Option.

lesson.md: A **case class** groups values that belong together into a new type. `case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)` defines a type `Point` with two **fields**, `x` and `y`. You create a point with `Point(3, 4)` and read a field with a dot: `p.x`. `println` shows the class name and the values.

lesson.code:
case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)

@main def run(): Unit =
  val p = Point(3, 4)
  println(p.x)
  println(p.y)
  println(p)

lesson.md: The fields of a case class cannot change. `copy` gives back a new object with some fields changed; the others keep their values. `==` compares two case class objects by their values.

lesson.code:
case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

@main def run(): Unit =
  val ana = Person("Ana", 30)
  val older = ana.copy(age = 31)
  println(older)
  println(ana == Person("Ana", 30))

lesson.md: A case class can have **methods**: functions that belong to it. Put a colon after the class header and write the methods below it, indented. Methods can use the fields directly. A method without parameters, like `area`, needs no parentheses.

lesson.code:
case class Rect(width: Int, height: Int):
  def area: Int = width * height
  def isSquare: Boolean = width == height

@main def run(): Unit =
  val r = Rect(3, 4)
  println(r.area)
  println(r.isSquare)

lesson.md: `match` can take a case class apart. `case Point(0, 0)` fits only when both fields are `0`. `case Point(x, 0)` fits when `y` is `0` and gives the first field the name `x`. `_` fits any value.

lesson.code:
case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)

def describe(p: Point): String = p match
  case Point(0, 0) => "origin"
  case Point(x, 0) => s"on the x axis at $x"
  case Point(_, y) => s"y is $y"

@main def run(): Unit =
  println(describe(Point(0, 0)))
  println(describe(Point(5, 0)))
  println(describe(Point(2, 7)))
lesson.output:
origin
on the x axis at 5
y is 7

lesson.md: Sometimes a value can be missing. An `Option[Int]` is either `Some(value)`, when there is an `Int`, or `None`, when there is nothing. The type in square brackets says what the `Option` can hold. `find` gives back the first element that fits, as an `Option`. `getOrElse` gives the value inside, or a default for `None`.

lesson.code:
@main def run(): Unit =
  val nums = List(4, 9, 12)
  val big = nums.find(_ > 5)
  val huge = nums.find(_ > 50)
  println(big)
  println(huge)
  println(huge.getOrElse(0))

lesson.md: You can use `match` on an `Option`, too. `case Some(v)` fits when there is a value and gives it the name `v`. `case None` fits when the value is missing.

lesson.code:
def half(n: Int): Option[Int] =
  if n % 2 == 0 then Some(n / 2) else None

def show(o: Option[Int]): String = o match
  case Some(v) => s"got $v"
  case None => "nothing"

@main def run(): Unit =
  println(show(half(10)))
  println(show(half(7)))

lesson.md: When a function gives back an `Option`, its type tells you that the value can be missing. You cannot use an `Option[Int]` like an `Int`; you must first handle both cases, for example with `getOrElse` or `match`. This prevents many errors.

`==` compares case class objects by their values. Both points have `x = 1` and `y = 2`, so they are equal.
